open-question.question: With milestone numbers gone, does the contributor flow in `CONTRIBUTING.md` still have the maintainer define a contributor's milestone on `main`, or does the contributor define it on the branch with `--at`, given that the reservation existed to keep numbers unique, and that two scopes may now hold the same slug while one scope refuses a duplicate?
open-question.recommendation: The definition commit on main is the one reservation a tool enforces: while the directory stands there exclusive creation refuses the same path, and the branch's finish removes it through an ordinary merge, so no two milestones can share a path in history; an issue comment or a contributor-side check enforces nothing.
open-question.alternative: The reservation step stays, rewritten for paths: on accepting the proposal the maintainer runs `/define-milestone-goal --at <scope>` with the accepted goal on `main`, choosing the scope, and its `Milestone-definition: <path>` commit is the reservation. The contributor branches from that commit and runs the pipeline with `--milestone <path>`. The `/goto-next-milestone` step and the pointer conditions on reserving and merging go. An abandoned contribution is still cleaned up by reverting the definition commit. The pull request template's milestone field names the reserved path. Nothing else can take the contributor's path on `main` from acceptance until the merge. While the directory stands in `main`'s tree, the definition tool's exclusive creation refuses any later definition of the same path there. The branch's finish then removes the directory through an ordinary merge, so the one conflict check the shape keeps covers the contribution's whole life. The contributor also starts from the same kind of commit as today. The reason the reservation existed, unique numbers, is gone, but `main` still pays one definition commit per accepted proposal and the maintainer still runs a step. An abandoned contribution leaves a defined milestone on `main` that `live` lists until someone reverts it. It holds no scope, but nothing else prompts the revert now that `goto-next-milestone` no longer activates it. The placement is the maintainer's choice made at acceptance, not the output of the contributor's `discuss-milestone-goal` step, which this flow skips.

The reservation step goes, as the draft's step 3 says. Acceptance is a reply on the proposal issue and writes nothing to `main`. The contributor branches from `main`, runs `/discuss-milestone-goal` to get the placement, then runs `/define-milestone-goal --at <scope>` on the branch, and runs the pipeline through finish with the path that definition printed. The flow makes no check of the path against `main` or any other branch. The pull request template's milestone field names the path the branch defined. It is the simplest flow and matches the draft. `main` gets no commit until the merge, and an abandoned contribution leaves nothing to revert. The contributor runs the whole pipeline, placement included, exactly as a maintainer would on their own milestone. Nothing stops the same path from being defined on `main` or on another contributor's branch at the same time. The branch creates the directory and its finish removes it, so the merge changes nothing at that path and raises no conflict. The result is two different milestones under one path in history: their `Milestone-finish: <path>` subjects collide, and `tasks`, `milestones`, and `summary` on that path mix both records. This silently breaks the draft's claim that subjects naming a path stay unique.

The reservation step goes and the contributor defines on the branch with `--at`, as in the no-coordination flow, but `CONTRIBUTING.md` adds one check before the definition. The contributor confirms that the path the definition will create has never been used on `origin/main`: it is not in `main`'s tree and no commit there touched it. If it has, the contributor picks a different title or scope. Nothing is written to `main` before the merge. It catches the common collision, a path `main` already holds or once finished under, with no maintainer step and no commit on `main`, and it keeps the contributor's own placement and definition. The check only sees `main` at the moment it runs and lives only in contributor prose that no tool enforces. A same-path definition that lands on `main` or another branch afterwards still produces the silent history collision at merge. The contributor also has to work out the slug the definition tool will derive from the title before running it.

The reservation moves from a commit to the acceptance itself. In the accepting reply on the proposal issue the maintainer names the milestone's full path: its scope and the title whose slug the definition tool will derive. The maintainer then avoids that path on `main` until the pull request merges or is closed. The contributor branches from `main` and runs `/define-milestone-goal --at <scope>` with that title on the branch, so the printed path matches the one named. Nothing is written to `main` before the merge, and the pull request template's milestone field names that path. The maintainer, who sees `main` and every open proposal, coordinates paths across concurrent contributions without a commit on `main` and without anything to revert when a contribution is abandoned. The reservation is an issue comment that no tool reads. A maintainer definition, or a contributor whose title derives a different slug, can still collide silently. The placement is fixed at acceptance, ahead of the contributor's `discuss-milestone-goal` step, and the maintainer takes on manual bookkeeping of the paths promised in open proposals.

open-question.question: What does the `gate` query print and exit with when another started milestone overlaps the named milestone's scope, given that the draft proposes the holders one path per line on stdout with exit 1, that every sibling tool's non-zero exit is one `Error:` line on stderr, that a runner chains the gate ahead of its write behind `&&`, and that a held scope is a wait rather than a failure?
open-question.recommendation: A held scope is a wait, not a failure, so the gate stays an ordinary query under the unchanged contract, holders as bare copyable paths with exit 0 and only a failure on an Error line, and the runner tests the print for empty as derive-tasks already tests list, in a separate step no bare chain can run past.

The gate holds only through the runner's test for empty output, made either inside the one shell call (the print captured and tested empty ahead of the write behind `&&`) or as a separate check step before the write, as `derive-tasks` step 2 already tests `list` for empty. It needs no exception to the shared output contract and reads a held scope as what it is, a no-failure result like the commit tool's exit-0 no-op, while keeping bare paths ready to copy; the tool stays a pure query that any reader, the next milestone's starting-state refresh included, can call without its print being treated as an error. A bare `gate && <write>` chain proceeds straight through a held scope, so the gate's force rests on every site carrying the emptiness test exactly; a site that drops it, or a runner that rewrites the call, silently defeats the sequencing the pointer used to hold, and each chained form adds a captured value to the call.

The draft as written. A held scope prints the holders on stdout, one bare milestone path per line in the canonical printed form, and exits 1; a clear scope prints nothing and exits 0; every failure stays one `Error:` line on stderr with exit 1 and nothing on stdout. Held and failed share the exit status and are told apart by which stream printed. The tool's output and error contract gains one stated exception for `gate`. A runner chains `gate && <write>` with no shell test of its own, so the write never runs on a held scope, and each holder line is exactly the string a later `--milestone` or finish call takes, ready to copy from beneath the stop line. It breaks the contract every sibling tool keeps, under which exit 1 always means one `Error:` line on stderr and nothing on stdout: a runner or harness reading the exit status alone cannot tell a wait from a broken git, and every call site has to inspect the streams to pick between its held stop line and its failed-check stop line.

Exit semantics as the draft's (held exits 1 with the holders on stdout, clear exits 0 printing nothing, failures one `Error:` line on stderr with exit 1), but each holder is printed as its own `live` query line verbatim rather than as a bare path, so the stop shows the holder's title beside its path in the same field order and separator `live` uses. It carries the same shared-exit-1 break of the sibling contract as the draft, and it ties the gate's print to the `live` line's fields, so whatever the Live line fields question settles (the started marker, which is redundant on a holder that is by definition started, included) is printed here too; a copy of the path means cutting one field out of a tab-separated line.

open-question.alternative: A held scope prints the holders on stdout, one bare path per line, and exits with a dedicated status reserved for "held" (for instance 3, clear of argparse's 2 and git's 128); a clear scope prints nothing and exits 0; every failure stays one `Error:` line on stderr with exit 1, exactly as every sibling tool's. The contract states the new status as the gate's one addition. Exit 1 keeps its plugin-wide meaning of a failure with an `Error:` line, the `&&` chain still stops the write on a held scope, and the call can tell a wait from a failure by status alone, so a fixed call or a harness branches on the code and never reads a stream or an error's wording. A dedicated held status (for instance 3) as in the previous option, clear exiting 0 with nothing printed and failures one `Error:` line on stderr with exit 1, but each holder printed as its `live` query line verbatim rather than a bare path. It keeps exit 1's sibling-wide meaning and status-only branching while giving the operator the holder's title in the stop, in the one line shape the `live` query already prints. It pays both costs at once: a new exit status branched on at every site, and a print bound to whatever the Live line fields question settles for `live`, with a started field that is always the same on a holder and a path that has to be cut out of the line to be copied.

`gate` is an ordinary query exiting 0 whether held or clear, as in the previous option, with only a failure exiting 1 on one `Error:` line, the runner testing the print for empty; each holder is printed as its `live` query line verbatim rather than a bare path. No contract exception and no new status, and the stop shows each holder's title in the one line shape `live` prints, so `gate` reads as `live` narrowed to the overlapping started milestones. It keeps the exit-0 option's risk that a call missing the emptiness test runs its write through a held scope, and adds the dependence on the Live line fields question's outcome, with a redundant started field and a path to cut out of each line.

A held scope is reported as a refusal under the unchanged contract: one `Error:` line on stderr naming every holder's path within that one line, nothing on stdout, exit 1; a clear scope prints nothing and exits 0; every other failure is likewise one `Error:` line with exit 1. Each runner stops on one fixed line for a refused gate whatever the cause, with the tool's `Error:` line verbatim beneath it. Nothing in the tool family's contract changes and each site has exactly one gate condition and one stop line, the `&&` chain stopping the write on either cause, in line with the convention that a refused tool call is one condition whose `Error:` line tells the reasons apart. It rejects the premise that a held scope is a wait rather than a failure: the fixed line no longer tells a harness whether to wait for a holder's finish or to repair the environment, which only the error's wording now says and which no runner may classify, and the holders arrive folded into one line instead of one path per line to copy.

open-question.question: Which fixed milestones-tool call replaces the `milestones/README.md` history read in `discuss-milestone-goal` step 1 and in `ask-in-milestone-context`, and with what bound, given that the draft names `record .` as the whole project's history, that this repository's history holds 53 milestones with 3 to 8 bullets each, and that both skills read the whole history section today?

recommendation.option: Whole record to discuss, scoped record to ask

open-question.recommendation: Goal discussion runs once per milestone and is where a missed past decision costs most, so it keeps today's whole-history depth through one fixed record call, while the question-driven skill pays per question for the path-scoped slice it needs, as its read-only-what-the-question-needs rule already has it.

alternative.id: Whole record to discuss, scoped record to ask

The question-driven skill, which may be invoked many times per milestone, pays only for the slice each question needs. `discuss-milestone-goal` takes the unbounded, ever-growing read with all the cost of the whole-record option, already above today's 103 KB. The discretionary `ask-in-milestone-context` read cannot be pinned by a test, and the two sites differ in shape. The size of both reads depends on the Record composition question, and `ask-in-milestone-context`'s reach to past work depends on the Ask-context without milestone question.

One call shape serves both sites and a test can pin it. The read grows with the project and never gets smaller. Today's history section is already 507 lines and about 103 KB, read on every invocation of either skill. `record .` adds about 180 task lines on top, and every new milestone adds its summary and its tasks. Its exact size and shape hang on the Record composition question (print shape, and whether `record .` is bounded by the tool itself).

Then, at the runner's own judgment, they run `summary <path>` for each listed milestone whose title and date say it bears on the goal or the question. The fixed cost is one short line per milestone (53 lines for this repository's history). It grows slowly and is cheap enough to need no bound, so no milestone is cut off. Summaries are paid for only where a title says they matter, and both conversational readers then follow the same pattern as the review pass. A title alone can hide relevance, so a milestone whose bullets would have shown a dependency or conflict may never get its summary read. The depth of the read is left to runner judgment, which no test can pin. Each drill costs an extra turn. It reads less than today's whole history read. The line's content depends on the Milestones query line question, and what each drill shows depends on the Live summary print question.

Both skills run one fixed, unconditional, unbounded call through a summaries-only form of the milestones tool: the `milestones .` line of every milestone with its finish summary beneath it and no task lines (for example a `--with-summary` flag, following the `tasks --with-body` model). open-question.recommendation: The breaking release is the first whose notes the old reader cannot gather, so its reader should exist before it is needed, and reading the finished milestones and their summaries through the tool parses the body contract and the trailer rule in one place rather than a second time in plain git.
open-question.alternative: This milestone carries a task that rewrites step 5a–5e of `/release-plugin` to read the record through the milestones tool's history queries, not through a `git log` of its own. `milestones .` supplies the finished milestones with their finish dates, the skill keeps those finished after the last tag's date, and `summary` on each one supplies its title line and bullets for that milestone's `###` section. The README cross-check is dropped, and steps 3c and 7, which read `CHANGELOG.md`, stay as they are. Release notes read the finish records through the same tested parser as every runtime reader (`discuss-milestone-goal`, `ask-in-milestone-context`). The body contract and any trailer rule are then parsed in one place only, so a later change to the finish body cannot quietly break the release notes. A maintainer-only skill outside `core/` comes to depend on a tool's command path and on line shapes this milestone is still settling (the Milestones query line, Live summary print, and Trailer in finish body axes), so the rewrite can only be written once those land. It still depends on migrated commits carrying the original finish dates (the Migration commit mechanism axis), and it adds a task to a milestone of about fourteen tasks whose Goal does not name the release skill.

This milestone carries a task that rewrites the note gathering in `/release-plugin`. That gathering is step 5a–5e: 5a takes the commit side from `Milestone-finish:` subjects path-scoped to `milestones/README.md`, 5b takes the history side from a diff of the README's `### Milestone` headings, 5c cross-checks the two, and 5e reads each README entry. Steps 3c and 7 read only `CHANGELOG.md` and stay as they are. The new gathering reads the finish commits directly with the skill's own `git log`: it takes every `Milestone-finish: ` subject with its body, keeps a milestone when the commit's author date is later than the last tag's, and builds each `###` section from the body's title line and bullets. The README cross-check is dropped, because the finish commit becomes the only record and there is no second side to compare. The skill's other README mentions, such as the zsh example `$LAST_TAG:milestones/README.md`, are reworded in the same task. The milestones tool is not used. The breaking release is the first one whose notes the old reader cannot gather, and with this option its reader exists and is tested before it is needed: in the range 1.9.0..HEAD it collects milestones 51–53 through their migrated bodies and 54 through its native body. The skill also stays as self-contained as it is today, using plain git commands like every other step and calling no plugin tool. The selection depends on migrated finish commits carrying the original finish author dates. The commit range alone would also pick up the migration's commits for milestones 1–50, which earlier releases already covered. So this option depends on how the migration sets its dates (the Migration commit mechanism and Migration missing finish date axes). It also parses the body contract a second time, outside the tool, including how a trailing attribution block is handled (the Trailer in finish body axis). And it adds a task to a milestone sized at about fourteen tasks, whose Goal names commit subjects, chains, host trees, docs, and `CLAUDE.md` but not the release skill.

This milestone rewrites `/release-plugin` so that finish records stop feeding the release notes. The skill's empty-range path (step 5d, which condenses the range's commit subjects, and their bodies where a subject is unclear, into bulleted notes) becomes the only way notes are composed. Steps 5a–5c and 5e, along with every README read, are removed, and steps 3c and 7 stay as they are. Neither the README nor the finish commit bodies are read for notes. The release notes no longer depend on the finish body contract, on migrated author dates, or on any milestones-tool query shape. The rewrite can therefore be written now, independent of every sibling still open, and it cannot break when the record's shape changes again. The notes lose the per-milestone `### <Title> (milestone N)` sections that every release since 0.9.8 has carried. Each release instead has to condense hundreds of commits, most of them annotation and answer commits, which repeats work the finish summaries already did. This option also ignores the finish summary written for the record, the only text in the record written for exactly this purpose.

This milestone leaves `.claude/skills/release-plugin/SKILL.md` unchanged and gives it no task. The note gathering is rewritten later, outside this milestone, before the next release is cut: either in a maintainer commit made when that release is prepared, or in a later milestone ahead of it. That rewrite also decides the reader's source and selection rule. Until it lands, `/release-plugin` stops at its step 5c cross-check, with nothing changed and nothing published. Once the migration removes `milestones/README.md`, the history side reads no headings, while the commit side still finds milestones 51–53's old finish commits in the range. The milestone keeps exactly the scope its Goal states and cuts no release. The skill is rendered into no host tree and reaches no user project, so nothing a user runs depends on it in the meantime. The rewrite can also be written against the queries and finish bodies as they actually landed, and tried on the real range when the release is cut. The breaking release is the one whose notes have to name the upgrade step, and with this option it is the first run of a reader nobody has written or tried. Meanwhile the tree carries a maintainer skill that is known to stop at its own cross-check. The design draft also lists "the release notes follow" among this milestone's pieces, so deferring leaves that piece undone with no recorded owner.
